stem: Write one equation each for (i) the Finkelstein reaction, (ii) the Wurtz–Fittig reaction.
model_answer:
(i) $\ce{CH3CH2Br + NaI ->[dry acetone] CH3CH2I + NaBr}$ [1]
(ii) $\ce{C6H5Cl + CH3Cl + 2Na ->[dry ether] C6H5CH3 + 2NaCl}$ [1]
hint: Finkelstein: NaI in dry acetone. Wurtz–Fittig: one aryl and one alkyl halide with sodium in dry ether.

label: PYQ-style
stem:
In each pair, which compound reacts faster, and why?
(i) S$_\text{N}$2: 1-bromobutane or 2-bromobutane
(ii) S$_\text{N}$1: $\ce{C6H5CH2Cl}$ or $\ce{C6H5CH(Cl)C6H5}$
model_answer:
(i) **1-Bromobutane**: it is a primary halide, so there is less steric hindrance to backside attack by the nucleophile. [1]
(ii) **$\ce{C6H5CH(Cl)C6H5}$**: its carbocation is stabilised by resonance with two phenyl rings, so it forms more easily. [1]

scheme.step: (i) **1-Bromobutane**: it is a primary halide, so there is less steric hindrance to backside attack by the nucleophile.
(ii) **$\ce{C6H5CH(Cl)C6H5}$**: its carbocation is stabilised by resonance with two phenyl rings, so it forms more easily.

hint: SN2: the less crowded carbon wins. SN1: the more stable carbocation wins.

stem:
How will you carry out these conversions?
(i) but-1-ene to but-2-ene   (ii) benzene to biphenyl   (iii) cumene to phenol
model_answer:
(i) $\ce{CH3CH2CH=CH2 ->[HBr] CH3CH2CH(Br)CH3 ->[alc. KOH][\Delta] CH3CH=CHCH3}$ [1]
(ii) $\ce{C6H6 ->[Cl2][anhyd. FeCl3] C6H5Cl}$; $\ce{2C6H5Cl + 2Na ->[dry ether] C6H5-C6H5 + 2NaCl}$ [1]
(iii) Cumene $\ce{->[O2]}$ cumene hydroperoxide $\ce{->[H+][H2O]}$ phenol + propanone [1]
hint: (i) Add HBr, then eliminate (Zaitsev). (ii) Chlorinate, then Fittig. (iii) Air oxidation, then dilute acid.

label: PYQ-style
stem:
(a) Give two reasons why haloarenes are much less reactive than haloalkanes towards nucleophilic substitution. [2]
(b) Name the major alkene formed when 2-bromopentane is heated with alcoholic KOH, and the rule that predicts it. [1]
model_answer:
(a) (i) **Resonance**: a lone pair of the halogen is delocalised into the ring, giving the C–X bond partial double-bond character, so it is harder to break. [1]
(ii) **Hybridisation**: the carbon bonded to halogen is sp$^2$ (more electronegative than sp$^3$), so the C–X bond is shorter and stronger. (Also acceptable: the phenyl cation is not resonance-stabilised; the electron-rich ring repels the nucleophile.) [1]
(b) **Pent-2-ene** is the major product, by **Zaitsev's rule** (the alkene with more alkyl groups on the doubly bonded carbons is preferred). [1]

scheme.step: (a) (i) **Resonance**: a lone pair of the halogen is delocalised into the ring, giving the C–X bond partial double-bond character, so it is harder to break.

(ii) **Hybridisation**: the carbon bonded to halogen is sp$^2$ (more electronegative than sp$^3$), so the C–X bond is shorter and stronger. (Also acceptable: the phenyl cation is not resonance-stabilised; the electron-rich ring repels the nucleophile.)
(b) **Pent-2-ene** is the major product, by **Zaitsev's rule** (the alkene with more alkyl groups on the doubly bonded carbons is preferred).

hint: (a) Think resonance and hybridisation of the ring carbon. (b) Apply Zaitsev's rule.

label: PYQ-style
stem: *Nucleophilic substitution of haloalkanes follows two main pathways. In S$_\text{N}$2 the nucleophile attacks the carbon from the side opposite the leaving group in a single step. In S$_\text{N}$1 the C–X bond first breaks to give a carbocation, which is then attacked by the nucleophile. The stereochemical result, studied with optically active haloalkanes, is different in the two cases.*

parts.stem: What happens to the configuration when ($-$)-2-bromooctane reacts with NaOH by the S$_\text{N}$2 path?
parts.model_answer: The configuration is **inverted**: the product is (+)-octan-2-ol, with the –OH on the side opposite to where Br was. [1]

scheme.step: The configuration is **inverted**: the product is (+)-octan-2-ol, with the –OH on the side opposite to where Br was.

parts.stem: Why does an optically active haloalkane give a racemic product by the S$_\text{N}$1 path?
parts.model_answer: The carbocation intermediate is planar (sp$^2$); the nucleophile attacks from either face with equal ease, giving both enantiomers in equal amounts. [1]

scheme.step: The carbocation intermediate is planar (sp$^2$); the nucleophile attacks from either face with equal ease, giving both enantiomers in equal amounts.

parts.stem:
Arrange 1-bromopentane, 2-bromopentane and 2-bromo-2-methylbutane in increasing order of S$_\text{N}$2 reactivity, with a reason.
**OR**
What is a chiral molecule? Which of 1-chlorobutane and 2-chlorobutane is chiral? What is a racemic mixture?
parts.model_answer:
2-bromo-2-methylbutane (3$^\circ$) $<$ 2-bromopentane (2$^\circ$) $<$ 1-bromopentane (1$^\circ$). [1] More alkyl groups on the carbon bearing Br mean more steric hindrance to the approaching nucleophile. [1]

**OR**

A chiral molecule is one that is not superimposable on its mirror image. [½] **2-Chlorobutane** is chiral (C-2 has four different groups). [½] A racemic mixture contains equal amounts of the two enantiomers and has zero optical rotation. [1]

scheme.step: More alkyl groups on the carbon bearing Br mean more steric hindrance to the approaching nucleophile.

hint: The rate law gives the mechanism away: both reactants in it means SN2, the halide alone means SN1.
